checkpoints: The exact log (ZSET) keeps one entry per granted in-window request, giving exact counts at the cost of O(N) memory that grows with traffic.
The log costs O(log N + M) per check on hot keys, since each check touches the window's entries.
The approximate counter keeps only curr/prev integers and estimates prev * (1 - elapsedRatio) + curr, giving O(1) memory at roughly 0.003% error.
Choose the log when precision is contractual (billing, strict quotas, audit) and RAM proportional to traffic is acceptable.
Choose the counter for high-throughput limiting where sub-percent slack is harmless and constant memory per client is essential.
The counter's weakness is its uniform-spread assumption: it treats the previous window's traffic as evenly distributed over time.
The estimate drifts when the previous window was extremely bursty right against the boundary — that specific key should be promoted to the exact log when it matters.
Checking user → tenant → global (innermost first) rejects the narrowest tier — most likely the binding constraint — earliest, short-circuiting before broader counters are ever touched.
bump() always INCRs before knowing whether the next tier will accept, so innermost-first order also minimizes compensation work.
A reject at user undoes nothing; a reject at tenant undoes exactly one INCR (user's); a reject at global undoes two (user's and tenant's).

Reversing the order (global first) would let an abusive user touch the global quota before being stopped at a narrower tier, and every global rejection would then need to undo more work instead of less.
Compensation DECR guarantees each reject branch DECRs exactly the set of tiers it INCRed above it, so a rejected request consumes precisely zero quota.
Skipping a DECR fails silently: the rejected request still leaves its INCR mark on an inner tier.
That counter then reads higher than the number of requests actually granted, so the limiter quietly over-throttles with no exception or error log pointing at the cause.

The cascade also returns a diagnostic a flat counter cannot give — exactly which tier blocked the request (blockedAt: USER | TENANT | GLOBAL) — letting you explain to a tenant precisely why they were throttled.

In a Redis ZSET, the member is the unique identity of an entry while the score only determines its sort order for range operations — two `ZADD` calls with the same member do not create two entries, the second call simply overwrites the score of the existing one.

The given code calls `ZADD key now now`, using the millisecond timestamp `now` as both the score and the member, so any two requests that compute the same `Date.now()` value collide on the exact same member.

Because `Date.now()` only has millisecond resolution, a burst of concurrent requests can easily produce identical timestamps, making same-member collisions realistic under load rather than a rare edge case.

When a same-millisecond collision happens, the second `ZADD` overwrites the first entry instead of adding a new one, so only one member ends up stored in the ZSET for two requests that were actually granted.

The subsequent `ZCARD` call then reports one fewer entry than the number of requests truly admitted, so the limiter compares an undercounted value against `limit` and keeps granting requests past the configured threshold.

The fix is to keep the score as `now` — so `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE` window eviction still works correctly by time — while making the member unique per request, for example `${now}-${randomUUID()}` passed as the ZADD member argument.
Separating the ordering key (score) from the identity key (member) lets concurrent same-millisecond requests each occupy their own ZSET entry without breaking the time-based eviction logic.

Correctness can be verified by firing many requests concurrently within a single millisecond (e.g. `Promise.all` over `limit + 5` calls) and asserting that `ZCARD` equals the number of calls that returned `allowed: true`, with the `(limit + 1)`th request correctly denied.
Redis Cluster partitions the keyspace into 16384 hash slots and, by default, computes a key's slot as `CRC16(key) mod 16384` over the entire key string.

Three unrelated key names such as `quota:u:<userId>`, `quota:t:<tenantId>`, and `quota:g` share no common substring, so they almost certainly hash to different slots and can even be owned by different nodes.

A Lua script executed via `EVALSHA`/`EVAL` is only allowed to touch keys that all resolve to the same slot, because Redis needs that guarantee to run the script atomically and single-threaded on one node without cross-node coordination.

When keys span multiple slots, Redis Cluster rejects the command outright with `CROSSSLOT Keys in request don't hash to the same slot`, which is exactly why the endpoint 500s on every call once deployed to a cluster.

Standalone Redis has no concept of hash slots — every key lives on the same single node — so a multi-key script over `quota:u:*`, `quota:t:*`, and `quota:g` works there by accident, not because the key naming is correct.

A hash-tag fixes this by wrapping the substring the keys should share — here the tenant id — in curly braces, e.g. `` `{q:${tenantId}}:u:${userId}` ``, `` `{q:${tenantId}}:t` ``, `` `{q:${tenantId}}:g` ``.

Redis Cluster's slot-hashing rule has a special case: when a key contains a `{...}` substring, only the text inside the first pair of braces is hashed, so all three keys sharing the same braced tag land on the same slot and node and the multi-key script becomes atomic again.

Forcing all of a tenant's keys onto a single slot via a shared hash-tag concentrates that tenant's entire quota traffic onto one node, so a very large tenant can turn that node into a hot spot; the standard mitigation is to sub-shard the tag (e.g. append a bucket to the tag) for such tenants, at the cost that cross-bucket state for that tenant is no longer atomic in a single script.

Calling `ZADD` unconditionally, before the `count < limit` check even runs, means the sorted set records every request that hits the key — accepted and rejected alike — instead of only the ones that actually consume quota.

When a client is flooded far past its limit, that unconditional `ZADD` keeps writing one new member per attempt into the ZSET regardless of the reject decision, so the set's memory footprint scales with total attempts rather than with the configured `limit`.
The count check itself is correct — it does gate the allow/reject decision properly — the bug is purely in the bookkeeping that happens one line earlier and independently of that decision.

The fix is to move `ZADD` inside the branch where `count < limit`, so the sorted set only gains a member when a request is actually granted, and to return early on the reject path without touching the ZSET at all.

Restructuring around a 'record-on-grant' rule bounds the ZSET to roughly `limit` entries per active client, since denied requests never get written, no matter how many times an abusive client retries.

The key also has no `PEXPIRE`, so a legitimate client that sends a few requests and then goes silent leaves its ZSET sitting in Redis forever — nothing ever reclaims it because `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE` only trims on the next call to that key, which never comes.
Calling `PEXPIRE(key, window)` right after every successful `ZADD` makes an idle key self-expire after one window of inactivity, closing the second, independent leak from the record-on-reject bug.

Verifying the fix means flooding one key with far more requests than its limit and asserting the ZSET's cardinality stabilizes near `limit` instead of climbing with the attempt count, then confirming the key's TTL expires it once traffic stops.
The mid-level answer optimizes 'where to store it', but the real design decision is 'what is the unit of storage'.
A single opaque, contiguous blob cannot tell whether this content is the same as something already stored, blocking dedup.
A single opaque, contiguous blob cannot tell which bytes are already uploaded, blocking resumable upload after a dropped connection.
A single opaque, contiguous blob cannot identify which independent piece can be fetched right now, blocking parallel transfer.
Fixed-size 1MB chunking cuts at constant byte boundaries, so chunk i is always the same byte range.
Per-chunk SHA256 turns content into an address, so identical chunks collapse into one copy, and each chunk is immutable and self-verifying.
A normalized file(1)→chunk(N) schema with a unique fileId+chunkIndex key makes each chunk independently queryable and ordered for reassembly.

Because both the split and the hashes are deterministic, re-uploading the same file yields the identical manifest, which is what lets a downstream layer skip an already-known hash or resume at the first missing chunk.
A cache inside the API (in-process or Redis) does not remove the fundamental problem: every client still reaches the origin process and its public port.
Scaling out more API replicas just multiplies connections to the database without cutting the repeated work the origin does for content that hasn't changed.
The real fix is a separate edge tier: a caching reverse proxy (nginx proxy_cache) sits in front and serves identical requests straight from the edge.
With that edge tier in place, the origin only ever sees the MISS traffic the edge could not answer itself.

Pair the edge cache with origin shielding — the origin publishes no host port and is reachable only on the internal network — so a client or attacker can never bypass the cache to hit the origin directly.

The cost of this design is that the edge becomes the only door and a critical path, so the edge tier itself must be made highly available (multiple edge replicas behind a load balancer with health checks).

A shared cache keyed only on `$request_uri` cannot distinguish between different logged-in users hitting the same path, so a personalized response stored under that key gets replayed to every later requester regardless of who they are.

Sending `Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600` on a per-user endpoint like `/me` tells any shared cache in front of the origin that the body is safe to store and reuse across clients, even though the body actually differs per session — that turns a caching config into a cross-user data leak, not just wasted cache capacity.

Responses that carry authentication state — a request with an `Authorization` header or `Cookie`, or a response with `Set-Cookie` — must bypass a shared/edge cache entirely; only genuinely public, unauthenticated GET responses belong in that cache.

Fixing the leak requires two coordinated changes: the handler must mark `/me` `private, no-store` (or omit `Cache-Control`, which defaults to non-cacheable), and the edge must add `proxy_cache_bypass`/`proxy_no_cache` keyed on `$http_cookie`/`$http_authorization` so authenticated requests never read from or write into the shared cache.

`proxy_cache_valid any 1h` applies the same hour-long TTL to every status code the origin returns, including 4xx and 5xx, so a single transient `500` gets pinned in cache and replayed to clients for an hour after the origin has already recovered.

Error responses should be given a much shorter negative-cache TTL than success responses, or excluded from caching altogether — caching a transient failure for as long as a valid success response turns a momentary origin blip into an extended, self-inflicted outage.

With `proxy_cache_lock off`, every request that arrives after a hot cache entry's TTL expires misses at the same instant and is forwarded to the origin concurrently, producing a stampede; turning `proxy_cache_lock on` makes nginx admit exactly one of those requests to refill the entry while the rest wait for it.

Proving the fix works takes concrete before/after evidence, not just a config read-through: requesting the personalized endpoint as two different authenticated users must return different bodies with no leakage between them, and forcing then repairing an origin error must show the edge stop serving the stale error once the shorter negative TTL has elapsed.

A synchronous SELECT to read the current offset followed by an UPDATE to persist the new one against the Postgres `upload_session` row runs on every single chunk PATCH, so on a multi-GB upload split into thousands of 1MB chunks, that pair of round-trips is multiplied thousands of times and dominates PATCH latency far more than the SHA256 hashing or the dedup lookup.

The offset is validated and advanced on every chunk, but it only needs to be durably persisted occasionally rather than on every write — treating every check as a durability event is what turns a cheap operation into a database bottleneck.

Splitting the offset into two tiers — a fast Redis key such as `upload:<sessionId>` for the live value and Postgres for the durable record — lets each PATCH validate and advance the offset with an O(1) Redis GET/SET instead of a Postgres findOneOrFail followed by an update.
Postgres still owns the durable `upload_session` row, but it is written for status and recovery purposes rather than being the thing every chunk's validation blocks on.

Redis in this design is a rebuildable hot cache, not a second source of truth: if the key evicts or Redis restarts mid-upload, the offset can be reconstructed from the committed chunk total already durable in Postgres and the Redis key reseeded before the next PATCH is served.

A cold or missing Redis cache costs only one extra reconstruction read against Postgres — it never corrupts or silently loses the tracked offset, because Postgres remains the authoritative record throughout.

This is the classic speed-in-the-hot-tier, durability-in-the-cold-tier trade-off: Redis buys low-latency validation on the hot path while Postgres continues to guarantee the upload can never lose or misplace its true progress.

Verifying the fix requires two checks: measuring PATCH latency before and after the split to confirm it drops from two Postgres round-trips to roughly one Redis round-trip plus an occasional durable write, and deliberately killing Redis mid-upload to confirm the offset rebuilds correctly from Postgres so the upload resumes at the exact right byte.

A fixed TTL with no jitter means every concurrent reader of the same hot key shares an identical expiry moment, so the instant that boundary passes, all of them see a cache MISS at the same instant rather than staggered over time.

This synchronized MISS is a cache stampede (thundering herd): each of the ~50k concurrent readers independently falls through the edge cache straight to the shielded origin at the same instant, instead of one request rebuilding the entry on behalf of the rest.

`proxy_cache_valid 200 60s` only governs when a cached entry goes stale — it says nothing about how many concurrent requests are allowed to react to that staleness by hitting the origin, so origin CPU/DB load spikes periodically in lockstep with the TTL rather than staying steady.

Request coalescing via `proxy_cache_lock on;` fixes the root cause by letting exactly one of the concurrent MISSes actually reach `/api/cdn/origin/:fileId/:chunkIndex` to rebuild the entry, while every other concurrent request for that same cache key waits on that single in-flight rebuild instead of independently calling the origin.

Pairing coalescing with `proxy_cache_use_stale updating;` lets the edge keep answering the other waiting requests with the still-cached, slightly stale chunk during the rebuild window, so those clients get an immediate 200 instead of blocking behind the lock until the single rebuild finishes.

The staleness this introduces is bounded to roughly one origin round trip — the time the single coalesced rebuild takes (the 150ms `readChunk` cost) — which is a deliberate, acceptable trade-off in exchange for turning tens of thousands of simultaneous origin hits into one.

Because the origin sets an `ETag` from the chunk's SHA256, the single coalesced rebuild request can revalidate as a cheap `304 Not Modified` instead of re-sending the full chunk body, making the one allowed-through request even cheaper than a full refetch.

The fix can be verified by driving concurrent load against the same fileId/chunkIndex exactly across a 60s expiry boundary: before the fix the origin sees a burst of roughly 50k hits at each expiry, and after adding `proxy_cache_lock` plus `proxy_cache_use_stale updating;` the origin sees roughly one request per key per refill cycle while `X-Cache` still shows a clean MISS-then-HIT/stale pattern with no error responses.
